summary: Causal abstraction formally defines faithfulness of an interpretation: a high-level causal model faithfully explains a network if it is an exact transformation or constructive abstraction of it (Rubenstein 2017; Beckers & Halpern 2019; Geiger 2025). Graded faithfulness is approximate abstraction (d_tau, aggregated similarity, interchange intervention accuracy). Completeness appears only as testing unmapped variables (Meloux 2026). No work applies causal abstraction to CoT or verbalized reasoning; the closest is CAuSE, for natural-language explanations of classifiers. Verbalization is lossy, which needs projected abstractions (Xia & Bareinboim). Unrestricted alignment maps make abstraction trivial (Sutter 2025), and explanations are non-identifiable (Meloux 2025), so a definition must fix the map class. Concept variables are identifiable in LLMs only under sparsity or paired-shift assumptions. Causal abstraction could cover faithfulness, completeness, counterfactual tests and, with an observer model, legibility. It does not cover honesty, scheming or steganography.

candidates.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
candidates.authors: Atticus Geiger, Duligur Ibeling, Amir Zur, Maheep Chaudhary, Sonakshi Chauhan, Jing Huang, Aryaman Arora, Zhengxuan Wu, Noah Goodman, Christopher Potts, Thomas Icard
candidates.venue: JMLR 26 (arXiv 2301.04709, first posted 2023 as 'Causal Abstraction for Faithful Model Interpretation')
candidates.formalism: causal abstraction over deterministic causal models with intervention algebras (hard, soft and functional interventionals)
candidates.formal_object: Exact transformation and constructive abstraction (high-level H faithful to low-level L under alignment); approximate transformation as graded faithfulness (Sec. 3.2); interchange intervention accuracy (Def. 48); LIME read as behavioural-only approximate abstraction.
candidates.assumptions: White-box low-level model (full access to internals and the ability to intervene); a proposed high-level model; an alignment (partition plus value maps); a distribution over interventions, a similarity function and a summary statistic for the graded version.
candidates.relevance: The reference formal definition of a faithful explanation as a simplification of the computation. It states that graded faithfulness has no single correct metric. A CoT could be cast as the high-level model H.

candidates.title: Approximate Causal Abstraction
candidates.authors: Sander Beckers, Frederick Eberhardt, Joseph Y. Halpern
candidates.formalism: structural causal models (Halpern-Pearl style deterministic and probabilistic causal models)
candidates.formal_object: tau-alpha-approximate abstraction: worst-case distance, over allowed low-level interventions and contexts, between lifting the low-level outcome via tau and running the high-level model on the lifted intervention. alpha = 0 recovers exact tau-abstraction.
candidates.key_formula: d_\tau(M_L,M_H)=\min_{\tau_U}\max_{\vec X\leftarrow\vec x\in\mathcal{I}_L,\ \vec u_L\in\mathcal{R}_L(\mathcal{U}_L)} d_{\mathcal{V}_H}\big(\tau(M_L(\vec u_L,\vec X\leftarrow\vec x)),\ M_H(\tau_U(\vec u_L),\omega_\tau(\vec X\leftarrow\vec x))\big);\ M_H\ \text{is a }\tau\text{-}\alpha\text{ approximate abstraction iff } d_\tau\le\alpha
candidates.assumptions: Known low- and high-level causal models; a surjective state map tau; a metric on high-level states; extended to probabilistic models with a distance over distributions.
candidates.relevance: Gives a worst-case graded faithfulness grounded in the Halpern-Pearl causal-model formalism. It is the most direct bridge to the user's actual-causality plans.

candidates.title: Abstracting Causal Models
candidates.formal_object: A hierarchy: exact transformation, then uniform transformation, then tau-abstraction (the intervention map omega is induced by the state map tau), then strong and constructive tau-abstraction. These are binary relations stating when a coarse model faithfully abstracts a fine one.
candidates.key_formula: (M_H,\mathcal{I}_H)\ \text{is a }\tau\text{-abstraction of }(M_L,\mathcal{I}_L)\ \text{iff }\tau\ \text{surjective},\ \exists\,\tau_U\ \text{surjective with}\ \tau(M_L(\vec u_L,\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y))=M_H(\tau_U(\vec u_L),\omega_\tau(\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y))\ \forall\,\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y\in\mathcal{I}_L,\ \text{and}\ \mathcal{I}_H=\omega_\tau(\mathcal{I}_L)
candidates.assumptions: Known deterministic or probabilistic causal models; the set of allowed low-level interventions; a surjective state map.
candidates.relevance: Supplies the exact (binary) faithfulness relation in Halpern's framework. It is what any approximate notion reduces to at zero error, and it composes with HP actual causality.

candidates.title: Causal Consistency of Structural Equation Models
candidates.authors: Paul K. Rubenstein, Sebastian Weichwald, Stephan Bongers, Joris M. Mooij, Dominik Janzing, Moritz Grosse-Wentrup, Bernhard Schölkopf
candidates.formal_object: Exact (tau-omega) transformation between SEMs: two models are causally consistent if they agree on the effects of all (well-specified) interventions after mapping states and interventions.
candidates.assumptions: Probabilistic SEMs; a state map tau and an order-preserving intervention map omega; a chosen set of interventions.
candidates.relevance: The original consistency criterion on which every later abstraction-based faithfulness definition builds. Geiger's exact transformation is a variant of it.

candidates.title: Causal Abstraction Inference under Lossy Representations
candidates.formalism: structural causal models, Pearl's causal hierarchy, graphical identification
candidates.formal_object: Projected abstractions, which drop the abstract invariance condition so that many low-level interventions with different effects may map to one high-level intervention. Includes translation of observational, interventional and counterfactual queries and a graphical criterion for identifying them.
candidates.assumptions: A low-level SCM or limited low-level data; a (lossy) abstraction function; graphical assumptions for identification.
candidates.relevance: Verbalizing reasoning is lossy: many internal states map to one CoT step. Standard abstraction is ill-defined there, so this is the needed extension for a CoT-as-abstraction definition.

candidates.title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?
candidates.authors: Denis Sutter, Julian Minder, Thomas Hofmann, Tiago Pimentel
candidates.formalism: causal abstraction with arbitrary alignment maps; impossibility result
candidates.formal_object: Proves that, under reasonable assumptions and with unrestricted (non-linear) alignment maps, any network can be mapped to any algorithm. It reaches 100% IIA even on randomly initialised LMs.
candidates.assumptions: Arbitrarily powerful alignment maps; the paper's stated regularity assumptions.
candidates.relevance: Any causal-abstraction definition of CoT faithfulness must restrict the class of alignment maps (an information-encoding assumption). Otherwise faithfulness is vacuous.

candidates.title: Everything, Everywhere, All at Once: Is Mechanistic Interpretability Identifiable?
candidates.authors: Maxime Méloux, Silviu Maniu, François Portet, Maxime Peyrard
candidates.formalism: statistical identifiability applied to causal-alignment explanations (exhaustive enumeration)
candidates.formal_object: Asks whether a unique explanation exists under mechanistic-interpretability criteria. Shows systematic non-identifiability: several circuits, several interpretations per circuit, several algorithms per network and several subspaces per algorithm.
candidates.assumptions: Small MLPs on Boolean functions; full enumeration of candidate circuits and alignments.
candidates.relevance: Faithfulness defined as abstraction does not single out one explanation. A CoT could be faithful alongside incompatible rival explanations, so the definition must say whether it requires uniqueness.

candidates.title: Validating Causal Abstraction Metrics on Simulated Complex Systems
candidates.authors: Maxime Méloux, Tiago Pimentel, François Portet, Maxime Peyrard
candidates.formalism: causal abstraction; benchmark of more than 30 observational, information-theoretic and causal metrics
candidates.formal_object: Causal Abstraction Error (CAE): a continuous validity metric for a high-level explanation that includes an explicit faithfulness test over unmapped low-level variables.
candidates.assumptions: Systems with ground-truth high-level explanations; the ability to intervene on mapped and unmapped variables.
candidates.relevance: Finds that only causal metrics separate valid from invalid abstractions, and only if unmapped variables are tested. That test is a formal handle on explanation completeness, the part a CoT leaves out.

candidates.title: Compositional Abstraction Error and a Category of Causal Models
candidates.formalism: category theory (enriched categories) over finite interventional causal models
candidates.formal_object: A category of finite interventional causal models whose abstraction errors compose: the error of an M to M'' abstraction is bounded by the sum of the step errors.
candidates.assumptions: Finite interventional causal models; a chosen distance between distributions.
candidates.relevance: A compositionality desideratum for graded faithfulness. It is useful if CoT faithfulness is defined through a chain of abstractions (network to features to verbal steps).

candidates.title: CAuSE: Decoding Multimodal Classifiers using Faithful Natural Language Explanation
candidates.authors: Dibyanayan Bandyopadhyay, Soham Bhattacharjee, Mohammed Hasanuzzaman, Asif Ekbal
candidates.formalism: causal abstraction via interchange intervention training (IIT)
candidates.formal_object: A natural-language explainer trained by interchange intervention against a frozen classifier. Theorem 1: under idealized conditions (identical weights and an injective encoder) the explainer is a causal abstraction of the classifier and vice versa. Also a causal-faithfulness metric.
candidates.assumptions: White-box access to the classifier; an idealized two-neuron linear setting for the Lemma; an injective encoder.
candidates.relevance: The only work found that ties natural-language explanations to causal abstraction formally. It does so for classifiers, not for an LLM's own CoT.

candidates.title: Position: Causality is Key for Interpretability Claims to Generalise
candidates.authors: Shruti Joshi, Aaron Mueller, David Klindt, Wieland Brendel, Patrik Reizinger, Dhanya Sridhar
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (seed list says ICML; the arXiv page gives no venue)
candidates.formalism: Pearl's causal hierarchy; identifiability up to equivalence class; causal representation learning
candidates.formal_object: Informally defines estimand, equivalence class and identifiability (estimand constant within a class, varying across classes). Maps interpretability claims to rungs L1-L3. Separates ontological faithfulness from instrumental adequacy (App. B.5). No theorem.
candidates.assumptions: A stated estimand and intervention class; CRL assumptions for recovering variables from activations.
candidates.relevance: Gives the vocabulary for a CoT-faithfulness definition. Faithfulness claims about what the model would have output are rung-3 counterfactuals, mostly unverifiable without controlled supervision. Also separates ontological from instrumental faithfulness.

candidates.title: Causal Differentiating Concepts: Interpreting LM Behavior via Causal Representation Learning
candidates.authors: Navita Goyal, Hal Daumé III, Alexandre Drouin, Dhanya Sridhar
candidates.formalism: causal representation learning; interchange interventions; identifiability theory
candidates.formal_object: Causal differentiating concept (Def. 2): a latent whose interchange intervention is necessary and sufficient to switch behaviour k to l. Latents identified up to affine maps (logit-linear assumption), and up to permutation and scaling with 1-sparsity.
candidates.key_formula: \text{(nec.) } \forall x_k\in C_k,x_l\in C_l:\ M_{z_k^s\leftarrow z_l^s}(x_k)\neq c_l\ (s\neq r);\quad \text{(suff.) } \exists x_k\in C_k,x_l\in C_l:\ M_{z_k^r\leftarrow z_l^r}(x_k)=c_l
candidates.assumptions: Access to LM activations; behaviour logit-linear in the latent concepts; 1-sparse concept differences between behaviour groups.
candidates.relevance: Gives a necessary-and-sufficient interchange criterion and conditions under which behaviour-driving concept variables are identifiable in LMs. These are the ground-truth variables a faithful CoT would have to mention.

candidates.title: Sparse Shift Autoencoders for Identifying Concepts from Large Language Model Activations
candidates.authors: Shruti Joshi, Andrea Dittadi, Sébastien Lachapelle, Dhanya Sridhar
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cited by the position paper as 'Identifiable steering via sparse autoencoding of multi-concept shifts')
candidates.formalism: causal representation learning; identifiability from paired observations
candidates.formal_object: Sparse Shift Autoencoders: sparse representations of embedding differences. Proved identifiable from paired observations that differ in multiple unknown concepts, but not all.
candidates.assumptions: Paired prompts differing in a sparse, unknown subset of concepts; access to activations.
candidates.relevance: Gives identifiability conditions for concept variables in real LLM activations. These are needed before 'the CoT reports the concepts the model used' can have a well-defined truth value.

candidates.title: Unsupervised Causal Abstractions Discovery
candidates.authors: Théo Saulus, Simon Lacoste-Julien, Dhanya Sridhar
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (seed list says UAI 2026 workshop)
candidates.formalism: causal abstraction; low-rank causal discovery; factor SCMs
candidates.formal_object: Thm 1: latents of a low-rank (factor) graph form a uniform transformation (abstraction) of the low-level SCM. Thms 2-3: factor graph and linear mechanisms identifiable up to permutation and affine maps. Thm 4 bounds approximate-transformation error.
candidates.assumptions: Low-level data generated by a factor SCM with a bipartite, strongly acyclic graph; anchors; linear parent mechanisms; Lipschitz mechanisms for the bound.
candidates.relevance: Learns the high-level model rather than testing a proposed one, with identifiability guarantees. This is a route to a reference abstraction against which a CoT could be compared.

candidates.title: Interpretability is in the Mind of the Beholder: A Causal Framework for Human-interpretable Representation Learning
candidates.authors: Emanuele Marconato, Andrea Passerini, Stefano Teso
candidates.formalism: causal representation learning with the human as an external observer; information-theoretic reformulation
candidates.formal_object: Alignment between a machine representation and the human's concept vocabulary, linked to interpretability through a 'name transfer' game. Disentanglement, concept leakage and content-style separation are recast information-theoretically.
candidates.assumptions: A causal model of the human's concepts and of the machine's representation; an observer model.
candidates.relevance: Adds the human receiver to the causal picture. This is needed to extend an abstraction-based faithfulness definition to legibility and simulatability, where the CoT must be readable by the reader as well as faithful.

candidates.title: Causal Abstractions of Neural Networks
candidates.authors: Atticus Geiger, Hanson Lu, Thomas Icard, Christopher Potts
candidates.formal_object: Aligns neural representations with variables of an interpretable causal model and uses interchange interventions to verify that they have the causal properties of the aligned variables.
candidates.assumptions: White-box network; a candidate high-level causal model; a hand-chosen alignment.
candidates.relevance: The first operational use of causal abstraction for neural networks. It is superseded formally by Geiger et al. 2025 and listed for completeness.

candidates.title: From Isolation to Entanglement: When Do Interpretability Methods Identify and Disentangle Known Concepts?
candidates.authors: Aaron Mueller, Andrew Lee, Shruti Joshi, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Dhanya Sridhar, Patrik Reizinger
candidates.formal_object: An empirical multi-concept evaluation. It uses standard identifiability definitions (weak identifiability, identifiability up to elementwise nonlinearity, App. C) and tests whether SAEs and probes recover and selectively steer correlated concepts. No new concept definition.
candidates.assumptions: Known ground-truth concepts with controlled correlations; access to activations.
candidates.relevance: Shows that features look disentangled correlationally but steering is not selective. Concept-level faithfulness claims therefore need interventional, multi-concept tests.

candidates.title: Who Guards the Guardians? The Challenges of Evaluating Identifiability of Learned Representations
candidates.authors: Shruti Joshi, Théo Saulus, Wieland Brendel, Philippe Brouillard, Dhanya Sridhar, Patrik Reizinger
candidates.formal_object: Defines identifiability up to a transformation class G (permutation-scaling, affine, elementwise nonlinear) and extends it to dimension mismatch. Proves that MCC and DCI give false positives or negatives outside their implicit assumptions (Props. 1-3).
candidates.assumptions: Known data-generating process and encoder geometry; m = d for the basic definition.
candidates.relevance: Warns that identifiability metrics are themselves misspecified outside their assumptions. This matters for any empirical check of a concept-level faithfulness definition.

candidates.title: Three Desiderata for Faithfulness in Machine Learning Explanations: The Case for Causal Abstraction
candidates.authors: Mette Friis Andersen, Maria Heuss, Ana Lucic
candidates.formal_object: Three desiderata for faithfulness (reverse-engineering specific behaviors, interventionist causal relations, appropriate model decomposition), argued to be met by causal abstraction.
candidates.assumptions: Adopts the causal abstraction framework; no new formal definition.
candidates.relevance: States explicitly that there is no agreed definition of faithfulness and argues for causal abstraction as the evaluation framework.
candidates.verified: abstract (opened in a browser; OpenReview blocks automated fetches)

gaps: Faithfulness of CoT or verbalized reasoning: no paper defines it as a causal abstraction between the reasoning text and the model's computation (CAuSE covers natural-language explanations of classifiers only).
Completeness and soundness of an explanation: formalized only operationally, as testing unmapped variables (Meloux 2026), not as a concept.
Post-hoc rationalization and plausibility: no abstraction-based definition. Geiger 2025 only notes that behavioural fidelity (LIME) is not internal faithfulness.
Lossy verbalization: projected abstractions exist (Xia & Bareinboim) but have not been applied to text-level explanations.
Monitorability, legibility, obfuscation, steganography, honesty, deception, scheming, sandbagging, introspection and self-report accuracy: no causal-abstraction definition found.
Seed 'Faithfulness through Causal Abstraction' (openreview.net/pdf?id=b0rXC856Sm) could not be opened (OpenReview browser challenge) and was not found by exact-title web search, so it is not listed.
